blocks.content: Let's walk through a real example and see how Decorator keeps things modular, flexible, and easy to extend.
1. The Problem: Adding Toppings to a Pizza
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Adding Toppings to a Pizza

blocks.content: Imagine you are building an ordering system for a pizza shop. You start with a basic Pizza object. Then the topping requests come in:
["Add cheese","Add olives","Add mushrooms","Any combination of the above"]
The Naive Approach: A Subclass for Every Combination

3 toppings already produce 7 subclasses. Add a 4th and you hit 15. The formula is 2ⁿ - 1.

blocks.content: Where This Falls Apart
1. Class Explosion 3 toppings give you 7 classes. 5 toppings give you 31. Most are just reshuffled copies of the same logic.
2. Rigid at Runtime Customer wants to remove cheese? You have to swap the entire object. No way to add or drop a single topping on the fly.
3. Violates Open/Closed Principle Add a new topping like pepperoni and you must create a new subclass for every existing combination that now includes it.
4. Duplicated Logic Cheese pricing lives in CheesePizza, CheeseOlivePizza, CheeseMushroomPizza and every other cheese combo. Change the cheese price and you are updating a dozen classes.
What We Actually Need
A better design should:

["Add or remove toppings independently and dynamically","Combine any toppings in any order without a new class per combo","Write each topping once and reuse it everywhere","Add new toppings by writing one new class, nothing else changes"]
items: Add or remove toppings independently and dynamically
Combine any toppings in any order without a new class per combo
Write each topping once and reuse it everywhere
Add new toppings by writing one new class, nothing else changes

blocks.content: This is exactly what the Decorator Pattern solves.
2. What is the Decorator Pattern?

The Decorator Pattern is a structural pattern that wraps an object inside another object to bolt on new behavior at runtime. Instead of reaching for inheritance, you layer functionality on top of the original without ever touching it.
Two core ideas define it:

1. Same Interface Every decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps. The client has no idea whether it is holding a plain object or something wrapped five layers deep. It just calls methods and gets results.

2. Dynamic Composition Decorators stack at runtime in any order and any combination you choose. You are not locked into decisions made at compile time you build the behavior you need, when you need it.

Real-World AnalogyThink of a plain pizza base. Add cheese. Add olives. Add mushrooms. Each topping enhances what came before without replacing it. Remove one and the rest stay intact. The Decorator Pattern works exactly the same way behaviors stack up around a core object, each one adding its own layer without disturbing anything underneath.

blocks.content: The Four Participants

1. Component Pizza The shared interface that every participant implements. Both the plain base and every topping wrapper implement getDescription() and getCost(). The client only ever interacts with this interface.
2. ConcreteComponent PlainPizza The starting point. It delivers the base behavior a plain pizza with a fixed description and price. Every decorator builds on top of this.

3. Decorator ToppingDecorator The abstract middle layer. It holds a reference to a Pizza object and forwards every call down to it. On its own it adds nothing it exists purely as the foundation for concrete decorators to extend.

4. ConcreteDecorators CheeseDecorator, OliveDecorator, MushroomDecorator The actual behavior layers. Each one intercepts the call, adds its own description and price on top, then passes the rest down to whatever it is wrapping. Stack three of these and each one contributes its piece before handing off to the next.
3. How It Works
Here is the Decorator workflow step by step. Each topping wrapper adds its own piece and passes the rest down to whatever sits beneath it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245786989-e7cc7488.png
Step 1: Create the base
The client creates a PlainPizza. This is the core object just a base with a fixed price and description.
Step 2: Wrap it in a decorator
The client wraps the plain pizza inside a CheeseDecorator. The decorator stores a reference to the plain pizza inside it.
Step 3: Stack more decorators
The client wraps the cheese decorator inside an OliveDecorator, then wraps that inside a MushroomDecorator. Each layer holds a reference to the one below it.
Step 4: Call the operation
The client calls getCost() on the outermost decorator MushroomDecorator.
Step 5: Decorators add their piece and delegate inward
MushroomDecorator passes the call down to OliveDecorator, which passes it to CheeseDecorator, which passes it to PlainPizza.
Step 6: Results bubble back up
PlainPizza returns 3.00. CheeseDecorator adds 0.50 and returns 3.50. OliveDecorator adds 0.30 and returns 3.80. MushroomDecorator adds 0.40 and hands 4.20 back to the client.

Instead of a subclass per topping combination, we write one class per topping and wrap them around each other freely.

blocks.content: What We Achieved

["Dynamic layering Toppings stack and combine freely at runtime","Modular design Each decorator handles exactly one topping and nothing else","No class explosion 3 toppings need 5 classes total, not 7 combination subclasses","Open/Closed Principle Add a new topping by writing one new class, nothing existing changes","Flexible ordering Any topping in any order is possible with zero extra code"]
items: Dynamic layering Toppings stack and combine freely at runtime
Modular design Each decorator handles exactly one topping and nothing else
No class explosion 3 toppings need 5 classes total, not 7 combination subclasses
Open/Closed Principle Add a new topping by writing one new class, nothing existing changes
Flexible ordering Any topping in any order is possible with zero extra code
